title: Heat Transfer in Nature

standard_code: Class 7, Curiosity Chapter 7: Heat Transfer in Nature
standard_text: Transfer of heat by conduction, convection and radiation; good and poor conductors of heat; sea breeze and land breeze; clothes for summer and winter; the water cycle, infiltration and groundwater (summary of NCERT Curiosity Chapter 7).

key_big: Heat moves by conduction, convection and radiation.
key_sub: Sea breeze by day, land breeze by night.
body_html:
How to think about it

Heat always flows from a hotter object to a colder one. In solids it moves by conduction: metals are good conductors, while wood, plastic, wool and air are poor conductors (insulators). In liquids and gases, heated parts rise and cooler parts sink, carrying heat by convection. Heat from the Sun reaches us by radiation, which needs no material.

By day the land heats faster than the sea, so a cool sea breeze blows towards the land; at night the land cools faster and a land breeze blows out to sea. Dark surfaces absorb more radiation, so we wear light colours in summer. The Sun's heat also drives the water cycle, and rainwater seeps into the ground to refill groundwater.

Example

A spoon in hot tea gets hot. How?

heat moves along the solid

Answer: conduction

Example

Noon at the beach: which breeze?

land is hotter by day

Answer: a sea breeze

Common mistakes

  • Mixing up sea breeze and land breeze.
  • Thinking dark clothes keep us cool.
  • Thinking radiation needs air.

faq.q: Why do woollen clothes keep us warm?
faq.a: Wool traps air, a poor conductor, so less body heat escapes.

faq.q: How does the Sun's heat reach the Earth?
faq.a: By radiation, which can travel through empty space.
